solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

blocks.note: first meaning: exaggerated and showy in manner
second meaning: a faction or side

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a theatre company; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for over-the-top, affected behaviour and a noun for a faction holding shared views.

blocks.note: surface reading: earn cash, profit from something
setter's reading: the word is printed in upper case, so it has been put into capital letters

explanation.walkthrough: The printed capitals are the trick: turning a word into upper case is one meaning, and profiting from a situation is the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To capitalise on something is to exploit it for profit, and to capitalise a word is to write it in upper-case letters.

blocks.note: first meaning: pining for someone absent, feeling lost without them
second meaning: gone astray, not to be found

explanation.walkthrough: The split comes after 'without': being lost without someone is to pine for them, and something lost cannot be found.
explanation.definitionFit: Missing a person means feeling their absence keenly, and a missing object is one that has gone astray.

clue.text: About to crack puzzle that's big, say

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: to fox is to baffle or puzzle; it is split open
re means concerning or about
ample means large or plentiful

explanation.surface: Someone describing how to break into a large puzzle, with an illustrative aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' at the end, used before an instance, is the definition; 'puzzle' is a verb here, meaning baffle.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Say' used before an instance means the same as the phrase introducing an illustration of a point.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the verb for lecturing goes round the other piece

blocks.note: to orate is to speak formally, to lecture
N is the symbol for the newton, the unit of force

explanation.surface: A thorough lecture about the life of Isaac Newton.
explanation.walkthrough: Newton here is the SI unit of force, abbreviated N, not the scientist.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornate means elaborately decorated, full of fine intricate work, which is what detailed describes in design.

clue.text: I'd be all upset over comedy western

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged
in cricket an over is a set of six balls, and its abbreviation is added at the end

blocks.note: these seven letters are rearranged
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Someone declaring they would be thoroughly upset by having to watch a comic cowboy film.
explanation.walkthrough: El Diablo is a 1990 comedy western film starring Anthony Edwards and Louis Gossett Jr.
explanation.definitionFit: El Diablo is the title of a 1990 TV film that sends up the conventions of cowboy movies.

blocks.note: surface reading: any qualification at all
setter's reading: the letter A stands for a specific British school exam, the one taken at eighteen

explanation.walkthrough: The 'A' looks like the indefinite article, but it is the name of the exam itself; A-levels are the British exams taken at the end of secondary school.
explanation.definitionFit: A-level is the shortened name of the British school-leaving examination, so a single letter A labels this qualification.

clue.text: Provide sandwiches I can freely give?

indicators.note: freely means without restraint, so these letters are not held in their given order
to sandwich something is to hold it between two layers, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: to ply someone with food or drink is to provide it
these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone offering to supply sandwiches for free, as a generous gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give' is a noun here, as in a rope having some give, not the verb of donation the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Give as a noun means springiness or capacity to bend under pressure, the same quality as flexibility.

indicators.note: something not finishing stops short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: an event is a happening, an occurrence

explanation.surface: An occasion that is still going on, refusing to wrap up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is not 'motionless' but the intensifier, as in still better.
explanation.definitionFit: Even and still both intensify a comparative, as in even better or still better.

indicators.note: carrying means holding something within, so the short word is held inside
sort means arrange, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something that has come to a halt of a kind while still continuing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: something postponed is a sort of stopped, yet it still carries on later.
explanation.definitionFit: Postponed means put off to a later time: halted for now, but to be resumed rather than cancelled.

blocks.note: surface reading: two shillings and sixpence, the old British half-crown
setter's reading: two numbers that together make up the number after seven, so each is a part of it

explanation.walkthrough: Two and six was pre-decimal British money, two shillings and sixpence; but 2 and 6 are also parts that add up to 8, and the answer is an old Spanish coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Pieces of eight were Spanish silver dollars worth eight reales, the classic pirate treasure coin.

clue.text: Evil guards heading for Orient Express

indicators.note: to guard is to surround protectively, so one piece encloses the other
the heading of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: vice is wickedness, evil
the first letter of Orient

explanation.surface: A villain on board the Orient Express, guarding a carriage, as in a murder mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: O goes inside VICE after the V. 'Orient Express' looks like the train, but 'Express' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To voice an opinion is to express it, putting it into words.

clue.text: Wee bairn does better after this

definitions.text: Wee bairn does better after this

blocks.note: surface reading: a small Scottish child improves in general
setter's reading: wee is a verb, to urinate, which the child does better after this tuition

explanation.walkthrough: Bairn is Scots for child, and 'wee' is the Scots for small; read as the childish verb for urinating, it points to the potty lessons.
explanation.definitionFit: Toilet-training is teaching a young child to use the potty, after which they relieve themselves properly.

blocks.note: surface reading: a chemically unreactive element such as neon or argon
setter's reading: gas is chatter, and inert means lazy or pointless

explanation.walkthrough: Chemistry is a red herring: gas in British slang is talk or chatter, and inert means doing nothing useful.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle gossip is aimless, inconsequential chatter, matching 'inert' as lazy and 'gas' as talk.

clue.text: I saw, or see, monarch astride horse

indicators.note: a rider astride sits with legs either side, so the outer pieces flank the middle one

blocks.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
gee-gee is a child's word for a horse
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual monarch abbreviation

explanation.surface: A puzzled observer: did I saw something, or see a king on horseback?
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a self-description: a lumberjack might say 'I saw'. Gee-gee is a nursery word for a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A logger fells and cuts trees, so the person speaking 'I saw' is describing their job.

clue.text: Wasted, I had spoken for favourite

indicators.note: spoken means said out loud, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: blew means wasted, as in blew one's money, and I'd shortens I had

explanation.surface: A drunk admitting they were wasted, speaking up for a favourite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' looks like slang for drunk, but it is blew, as in squandered; 'blue-eyed boy' is British for a favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A blue-eyed boy is someone's pet or favourite, treated with special indulgence.

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is written from bottom to top

blocks.note: prim means stiffly proper
lave is an archaic word for wash

explanation.surface: A fussy person insisting on doing the washing-up early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wash up' looks like a phrasal verb, but 'up' only signals the reversal in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Primeval means belonging to the earliest ages of the world, so very early indeed.

indicators.note: something tragic has met disaster and is ruined, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A son encountering assorted heroes from tragic drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tragic heroes' reads as a theatrical phrase; 'tragic' is actually the anagram signal applied to 'various'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saviours are people who rescue others from danger, which is what heroes do.

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: seven in Roman numerals
to tell someone to do something is to order them

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction to crack seven eggs to get their yolks.
explanation.walkthrough: The 7 looks like a cross-reference to another clue but is just a number, written in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitelli is the plural of vitellus, the biological term for the yolk of an egg.

clue.text: A desire to circle around bay

indicators.note: to circle something is to go all round it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: taken as written
love is desire or passion
c, short for circa, means around or approximately

explanation.surface: Someone wanting to sail round a bay along the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: C sits inside LOVE, after the L, with A in front. 'Bay' is a recess in a wall, not a stretch of coast.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcove is a recess set back in a room's wall, which is one sense of bay.

indicators.note: totty is a dialect word for dizzy or unsteady, so the letters wobble into a new order

blocks.note: these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An attractive blonde was once someone's date.
explanation.walkthrough: Totty is British slang for attractive women, but in older dialect it means dizzy or shaky, the anagram signal; 'dated' is old-fashioned, not went out with.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Old bean' is an old-fashioned British form of address between male chums, so a fusty term for a friend.

clue.text: A reply means we receive pens

indicators.note: to pen something is to shut it in, so the letters are held within the words before

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A letter explaining the method by which we get writing implements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' looks like writing tools, but it is the verb for enclosing, as in penning sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: An answer is a response to a question or letter, which is what a reply is.

indicators.note: possibly suggests one arrangement among several, so these letters may be put another way

blocks.note: these fourteen letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the film being shown is the old police drama Dragnet.
explanation.walkthrough: Dragnet was an American police series later made into a film; 'is' is part of the letters, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Streaming video is footage transmitted over the internet for viewers, a modern form of broadcast.

indicators.note: almost means nearly but not quite, so the final letter is cut

blocks.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, zero
grew means became, as in grew old

explanation.surface: The ugly duckling story told in reverse: a duck that nearly turned ugly.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck in cricket is a score of nought, so it gives O.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is a hideous giant from folk tales, the archetypal ugly creature.

clue.text: Prison camp starts to give up inmate

indicators.note: starts are the opening letters, so only the first of each following word is kept

blocks.note: first letters of these two words
an old lag is a long-serving convict

explanation.surface: A prison camp prompting an inmate to give up hope.
explanation.walkthrough: Lag is British slang for a convict, as in old lag.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulag was the Soviet system of forced-labour prison camps, and the word now names any such camp.

blocks.note: surface reading: describing the word at 2 down, a word for lost
setter's reading: the 2 down word with two (II) missing, which strips out all its vowels

explanation.walkthrough: Read 2 as 2 down's word: take it with its two I's missing (II is the Roman numeral 2) and only MSSNG is left, a word with no vowels.
explanation.definitionFit: A word without its vowels has none left, which is exactly what this adjective describes: lacking any vowel.

clue.text: Piece in each line of letters

indicators.note: in places one item inside another, so the gun goes within the abbreviation

blocks.note: ea is the usual abbreviation for each
a piece is slang for a handgun
RY is short for railway, a line

explanation.surface: A short piece of writing in every line of a set of letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' is gangster slang for a gun, not a bit of writing; the gun splits the abbreviation for each.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistolary novel is told through letters, so the adjective means relating to or written as letters.

blocks.note: first meaning: a short period, as in a cold spell
second meaning: a quick casual picture

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like an instruction to spell out a word; 'spell' is a period of time, as in a cold snap.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold snap is a brief spell of weather, and a snap is also a casual snapshot taken with a camera.
